Silicon Valley Parents Want Less Classroom Technology — and the Push Is Reaching Public Schools

28 Oct 2026, 01:49 PM IST · GlobeWire Daily Education Desk · Source: www.theguardian.com

Confirmed Facts and Background

Both private and public schools in technology-heavy regions are limiting classroom tech, according to reporting by The Guardian. German Gil, a software engineer who has worked at Netflix, Facebook, and GitHub, enrolled his daughter at San Francisco Waldorf, a private school where fourth-grade students bind books by hand instead of using screens. Kindergarten tuition is about $40,000 per year, and high school tuition is close to $60,000. The school’s executive director, Lauren Smith, said applications for early childhood enrollment have grown notably, with many new parents working in tech.

Parents in Mountain View, San Mateo, Palo Alto, and other California tech enclaves are pressing public districts to reduce screen time. In San Mateo, a union high school district taskforce examining AI in schools included at least two volunteers from large tech companies, including one in Google’s AI division, according to school board trustee Jennifer Jacobsen. Some districts have acted: San Mateo public schools stopped sending Chromebooks home with kindergarten through second-grade students and imposed a blanket cellphone ban for high schoolers. Mountain View schools are moving away from i-Ready, an adaptive reading and math program that has faced criticism for repetitive lessons and litigation alleging unauthorized student data sharing. A spokesperson for Curriculum Associates, which makes i-Ready, said the claims are without merit and that the company does not sell student data or use it for advertising. Palo Alto public schools have prohibited smart glasses.

A 2025 New York Times teacher survey cited in the report found that 99% of teachers said their students received school-issued devices, and 81% said screens are provided by kindergarten. Research referenced in the article suggests pen-and-paper learning supports retention better than screen-based learning, and critics argue excessive ed tech can weaken student-teacher relationships. David Monahan, campaign director of the advocacy group Fairplay, said there is much more public buzz around limiting children’s screen use than there was a few years ago.

Practical Implications

Families with financial means can choose low-tech private schools such as San Francisco Waldorf, which offers financial aid but remains expensive. Public-school parents are organizing through groups such as Schools Beyond Screens and asking districts to demand evidence that educational technology improves learning before signing multimillion-dollar contracts. District leaders face pressure to vet vendors, limit device use in early grades, and set cellphone policies, though the scope of change varies widely by community.

What Is Confirmed Versus Unknown

Confirmed: Tech industry parents are enrolling children in low-tech private schools and lobbying public districts; several Bay Area districts have rolled back specific devices or programs; national survey data indicate near-universal device issuance in U.S. public schools.

Unknown: Whether less-resourced districts can sustain screen-limiting policies without private-level funding; how the Trump administration’s school choice programs might affect public school budgets as families exit; and whether current rollbacks will measurably improve student outcomes.
